principle: Keep every tunable number out of the code
why: If values are hard-coded, every tweak means diving into code and going through a programmer, yet parameters keep being tuned for balance to the very end, long after the programmer's job is done. Code is the bones and parameters are the muscles: change the muscles and the same bones behave in drastically different ways.
how_to_apply: Have programmers read every value that might need tuning (attack power, speeds, decelerations, timings) from a parameter table kept outside the code that planners can edit at any time. Build characters or vehicles as parameter sets on one shared behavior, with only a few true types in code. When a mode needs different physics, give it its own parameter set. When the game's tempo changes, retune every parameter instead of porting old values.
anti_pattern: Writing tunable numbers directly into code; one person as the only one who can change values; carrying old values into a game whose speed changed.
example: A move with attack power 10, where the code makes the move happen and the 10 is a separate parameter (46). Kirby Air Ride's machines differ only by parameters apart from star versus bike types (59). Brawl's fighters needed a second jump and movement parameter set for the Subspace Emissary (108). Ultimate's raised tempo meant none of Smash for's parameters could be reused (160).
review_question: Can a designer change any damage, speed or timing value without touching code or waiting for a programmer?
keywords: parameters data-driven design tuning values hard-coded magic numbers spreadsheet config tables balance data designer tools

principle: Make the edit-and-test tuning loop a single button press
why: Tuning is where you iterate most, so it must be as efficient as possible. On the original Smash and Melee, one conversion took ten minutes even for the smallest tweak, plus a reboot, with hand-edited text files, so Sakurai wrote every parameter himself. With a fast pipeline, more people can tune more values more deeply, and the director can supervise instead of entering data.
how_to_apply: Build a conversion tool, for example a spreadsheet add-in, that pushes edited parameters to every active dev kit or test build in one press, without a reboot. Give planners and other team members access so a small tuning team can work while the director reviews. Back them with play testers who keep playing the current build.
anti_pattern: Multi-minute conversions and reboots per tweak; a director who enters all the data while also supervising, approving and marketing.
example: Bandai Namco Studios' Excel add-in updates all active dev kits with one button press (46). From Smash for 3DS/Wii U, a small team of planners took over parameter entry; on Ultimate Sakurai only supervised (135, 220).
review_question: How many seconds pass between changing a value and playing with it, and how many people can do it?
keywords: iteration speed hot reload live tuning pipeline conversion dev kits tools workflow fast iteration delegation

principle: Make parameters unmistakable with plain-language names, units and formulas
why: Several people usually tune parameters later, so each one's meaning must be crystal clear to anyone; terse names like X-velocity get misread. Specs and parameters do not work if you cannot convey speed, so units matter. Hiding rarely used fields reduces human error, and formulas keep related values in balance. You will not get far with tuning if you cannot explain things clearly.
how_to_apply: In specs, write each tunable as a bracketed plain-language phrase with a placeholder value, such as [Special startup X-velocity is O] and [Special X-deceleration is O/frame], under the rule that anything in brackets becomes a parameter, and keep a list pairing each phrase with its value. State a unit for every speed (pixels per frame for sprites, km/h or m/frame for real-scale 3D) and every time (frames at your target rate). Hide rarely adjusted fields in the editor, and link dependent values with formulas, such as one move at 1/2 another's power.
anti_pattern: Unitless values; cryptic labels; a flat sheet where every field looks equally important.
example: Sakurai's bracket notation for a dash that decelerates as it goes (68). Smash attack parameters in Excel with hidden fields and formulas (46). Mario's top speed of about 1 pixel per frame on a 256-pixel-wide NES screen; Kirby Air Ride speeds in km/h (84).
review_question: Could a new planner read any parameter's name and know what it does and in what unit?
keywords: spec sheets parameter naming units brackets notation formulas spreadsheet hidden columns documentation pixels per frame frames

principle: Keep game speed independent of frame rate and processing speed
why: Games use frames as their unit of time, and distance equals time times speed, so whatever counts time controls how far and fast everything moves. His NES and SNES games counted screen interrupts, so PAL versions at 50 fps ran at 5/6 speed. In Meteos, game speed was tied to processing speed, so late optimization sped the game up and made it harder than tuned. A dropped frame is not slowdown unless your logic makes it so.
how_to_apply: Drive game logic from a clock that does not depend on how many frames are drawn or how fast the processor runs. When diagnosing performance, tell frame drops (less redrawing) from true slowdown (the game itself running slower). Find every timing that still depends on processing speed (enemy speeds, time limits, decay timers). Lock processing speed and frame timing before final balance, and redo tuning if they change.
anti_pattern: Logic tied to a refresh rate that varies by region or platform; treating a performance gain as purely good when it also changes game speed.
example: NES/SNES PAL ports at 5/6 speed (5). Meteos became harder after late optimization (141, 74). The Mushiking pet got hungry faster on the production unit than on the dev board (92).
review_question: If the frame rate halves or the processor gets faster, does the game still run at the same speed and difficulty?
keywords: frame rate independence game speed slowdown frame drops PAL 50Hz processing speed timing bugs fixed timestep delta time

principle: Set the frame-rate target early and cut content until it holds
why: 60 and 30 fps differ both in look and in how smoothly they control. 60 is ideal; 30 is an acceptable standard because 60 costs about half your visual performance. For Smash on 3DS, Sakurai treated a stable 60 as an absolute must and pared things down until it held, where many 3DS games ran at 30 or dropped stereoscopic 3D. A faithful port can still lose its mood if it runs choppy.
how_to_apply: Choose the target at the start of the project, per game. Budget for the worst-case scene (the maximum number of characters and effects) rather than the average. When one platform is weaker, let it set the shared limits, and cut or simplify features rather than lower the target. Profile every stage or level at maximum load.
anti_pattern: Dropping to 30 fps or cutting a headline feature late to fit everything in; budgeting for typical rather than peak load.
example: Smash for 3DS: four players, stereoscopic 3D, items, Pokemon and Assist Trophies at a stable 60; Ice Climbers, two characters at once, were too much (135). Ultimate's roughly 115 base stages had to hold 60 with eight fighters on Switch (99). The NES Ghosts 'n Goblins kept every enemy in place but lost its smooth, creepy feel to a low frame rate (156).
review_question: Does the heaviest possible scene hold the frame-rate target on the weakest platform you ship on?
keywords: frame rate 60fps 30fps performance budget worst case performance target stable frame rate porting weaker hardware optimization

principle: Spend processing where players look, and cut what nobody sees
why: Console hardware is not as powerful as most people think, so you must decide which elements are major and which minor. Players mostly look at the center of the screen, foundations are usually off-screen, and fighters are often small. The less you process an object, the more of it you can put on screen. Fingers are complex for their size and particles always cost something, so every effect and joint competes for the same budget.
how_to_apply: Rank assets by how much they are actually seen and spend polygons and texture detail in that order: in front of the camera and on playable surfaces first. Set model budgets by on-screen size, raised for models also shown up close elsewhere. Build LOD only when the gain is worth the labor. Prefer cheap light and color work in the asset over heavy per-object shaders. Lock finger joints and swap a few pre-made poses. Use billboards for flashes, particles and simple objects. Allow playful details only when they meet deadlines and cost no performance.
anti_pattern: Detail nobody will ever see; over-investing in small on-screen elements; LOD by default; fully simulating every finger on crowded screens.
example: Smash stages put skysphere detail in front of the camera; Inkling's stage had backdrop car tires that turned, which he asked to tone down (44). Super Mario 64's rolling iron balls are billboards (153). The N64 Smash fighter was about 300 polygons, about 200 with three or more fighters (40).
review_question: Which costly elements in the busiest scene would players never notice if they were cheaper?
keywords: optimization performance budget LOD level of detail billboards particles polygon budget processing cost prioritization major minor elements

principle: Turn hard memory and processing limits into design tricks
why: Limits reward ingenuity: Super Mario Bros. delivered far more game than Mario Bros. with 40 KB against 24 KB. Kirby's Dream Land was designed mostly for 512 kilobits (64 KB), so art was shared and mirrored, and enemy movement was hand-authored to match terrain with no collision checks, which was wasteful to make but light on processing. All you can do is work within your game's limits and aim for the best effect possible.
how_to_apply: Decide which resource is scarce. If memory is, share and flip art, cap animation frames, store sprites as stacked bitplanes and compress runs. If processing is, trade memory for it with hand-authored paths or frame animations instead of simulation. On size-limited media, test compression on your biggest asset sets early before cutting content. When space or time is tight, use presets or placeholder art so the budget goes into behavior.
anti_pattern: Asking for more resources before trying technique; cutting content to a download before testing compression.
example: Waddle Dee and Waddle Doo share a back half, two characters in the ROM space of 1.5; Gordo is one image flipped; Coner and Cappy have no terrain collision (100). Kirby's defeat stars are hand-placed per frame (244). Ultimate's music fit in a quarter of Smash for's space on a cartridge capped at about 16 GB (160). Family BASIC's 2 KB of program space made its built-in character presets crucial (118).
review_question: Which resource is actually scarce in this build, and are you trading the plentiful one for it?
keywords: memory limits ROM budget compression sprite reuse mirroring flipping retro constraints processing budget hand-authored animation run-length encoding bitplanes

principle: Verify the final build on real retail hardware before sign-off
why: Sakurai tuned Mushiking on a custom dev board just under one square meter and never played the production handheld; probably because of a processing-speed difference, the pet gets hungry faster than planned and almost always wants food, adding unintended stress. Smash Ultimate's CPUs felt too hard at launch and he still does not know why. When you work with computers, sometimes there is no telling what you will get.
how_to_apply: Before sign-off, play the finished game on production units, not just dev kits. Compare timer-driven systems (hunger, fatigue, growth), time limits and enemy speeds against design values. Schedule a final difficulty pass after late optimization lands. When several team members independently report the same feel problem, treat it as real even without a cause.
anti_pattern: Tuning only on development hardware; assuming a build that worked on the dev board will behave the same on retail units.
example: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking's hunger rate (92, 141). Meteos' late speed-up (141). Smash Ultimate's launch CPU difficulty (141).
review_question: Has someone played the final build on a retail unit and checked every timing-sensitive value against the design?
keywords: retail hardware testing dev kit vs production final build verification timing differences difficulty regression sign-off

principle: Remove input and display lag from every test, demo and capture setup
why: Even a game with great response time is ruined by lag, and many people do not recognize lag when they see it. Display latency comes from picture post-processing; at 60 fps every 16.67 ms is a frame of delay. Sound can lag on its own through a home theater system. Lag and frame rate also change how heavy a button feels, so a laggy setup misleads tuning.
how_to_apply: Before any demo, playtest, event or capture, press jump in an instantly responsive 2D game on that exact setup and confirm the character moves the moment you press. Switch TVs to Game Mode or Low Latency Mode, or turn off every picture-enhancing setting. Check audio separately and try an analog connection or low-latency audio. Convert listed display times to frames. Check yourself instead of trusting that someone else did, and rule out display lag before retuning feel.
anti_pattern: Assuming a setup is fine because someone has played on it; judging lag with a 3D game; TV post-processing left on.
example: At E3 2018's Treehouse: Live, the Smash Ultimate setup's lag ruined the controls until Sakurai pointed it out (8). NES Kirby via Nintendo Switch Online as a jump test (8). Sakurai swapped to his low-lag recording monitor mid-session (156). Score-chasers seek out CRTs, which need no buffer (252).
review_question: Was the feel of this build judged on a display chain verified to add no lag?
keywords: input lag display latency game mode low latency mode TV settings response time audio latency demo setup events playtest

principle: Calibrate for every controller, platform and regional hardware variant
why: Every console's analog stick is slightly different, so the lowest tilt that registers has to be configured each time. Flick dashes cause accidental dashes, so Ultimate exposes sensitivity. A D-pad gives only 0 or 1, so an analog-dependent game cannot simply support it. The NES lacked the cartridge pins for expansion audio, so several games sounded different abroad. Confirm and cancel sit in different places by platform, and the same speed value gives different results on screens with different pixel counts.
how_to_apply: Set and test the stick dead zone per platform or controller. Expose sensitivity for gesture inputs like flicks. Before promising support for an input device, check whether your mechanics need analog values. List each target's audio, input and button conventions and provide fallbacks. Recheck raw pixel speeds on every resolution. Account for peripheral costs: a twin-stick add-on for 3DS added about 5% processor load, too much for a game already at the limit.
anti_pattern: One stick-sensitivity value for every console; relying on hardware features only some versions have.
example: Analog tilt sensitivity per console (19); adjustable flick sensitivity in Smash Ultimate (154); Smash cannot be played with a D-pad (175); Famicom versus NES expansion audio (239); a 3DS twin-stick peripheral that added about 5% processor load in Kid Icarus: Uprising (125).
review_question: Has each supported controller and platform version been checked for dead zone, button conventions and missing features?
keywords: analog stick dead zone tilt sensitivity controller calibration platform differences confirm cancel buttons hardware variants regional differences ports

principle: Build debug commands for the test setups you use most
why: Without the right debug features, the team spends time inventing workarounds. Teams use debug mode every day, so its convenience has a huge impact on productivity. A separate debug controller is a real pain to hunt down, and debug menus bloat easily.
how_to_apply: Add direct commands for frequent setups, such as setting every character to a chosen damage percentage. Put debug functions on button combinations of the normal gameplay controller. Include capture tools (pause, rotate characters, zoom, change camera angle). Regularly reorganize and prune the debug menu, and strip it from the release build.
anti_pattern: Workarounds like temporarily changing a move's damage to set up a test; a separate debug controller; a bloated, disorganized debug menu.
example: Before Smash could set damage directly, the team made Fox's forward tilt deal 100% damage (195). Screenshot of the Day was captured with debug pause, rotation, zoom and angle controls, though fighters could not be moved nearer or farther (195).
review_question: Can a tester reach any common test situation in a few seconds from the normal controller?
keywords: debug mode developer mode cheats debug menu test setup commands productivity QA tools screenshot mode

principle: Add view toggles that isolate exactly what you are checking
why: Capes and clothes hide poses, and older workarounds such as scaling or removing the cape were clumsier; the transparency feature did not take long to build. Per-element display toggles are, in his words, another must-have and were used often. Effects pack information into an instant, and collision has to be distinguishable from backdrop, so both need dedicated views.
how_to_apply: Add a dev-mode option to make any selected model part, or the whole model, translucent or hidden. Add an on/off toggle for every display element. Add a view that highlights every collision surface (his example marks them in red). Add slow-motion and background-off toggles for effect review. Make these views available to reviewers outside the team.
anti_pattern: Editing the model (scaling or deleting parts) just to inspect an animation.
example: Smash Ultimate's caped fighters checked with transparency; a 3D fighting game developer whose tools could disable clothes and swaying objects (217). Collision surfaces shown in red (30). Ultimate's effects recorded with slow motion on and backgrounds off (79).
review_question: Can a reviewer hide, fade or slow any element to see exactly the thing under review?
keywords: debug visualization display toggles transparency collision view slow motion isolate layers render toggles animation review tools

principle: Reuse debug tools for footage, screenshots and player-facing aids
why: Smash's reveal gameplay was recorded by team members using debug and replay features to find the best camera angles, then checked and restructured repeatedly. The Training Mode trajectory guide began as a debug feature Sakurai requested; he worried it might reveal too much but included it because it is easy to understand.
how_to_apply: Build replay playback with a free debug camera so trailer and screenshot shots can be re-framed from recorded play. Review debug overlays for ones that would teach players, weigh whether they reveal too much, and ship the clear ones in a training mode.
anti_pattern: Capturing trailer footage live with no way to re-shoot an angle.
example: Fighter reveal gameplay segments (163); the Training Mode trajectory guide and Screenshot of the Day (195); in-engine reveal footage captured by footage specialists (50).
review_question: Can a moment of play be replayed and re-shot from any angle, and which debug views would help players learn?
keywords: replay system photo mode debug camera free camera trailer capture footage screenshots training mode overlays

principle: Aim testing at the places where systems fight over control
why: Full coverage is impossible: Ultimate's 89 fighters give about 8,000 pairings before movesets, items, extra players, stages, hazards and spirits multiply in. A game that takes dozens of hours to finish might need thousands to tens of thousands of hours to test fully. Bugs cluster where one thing forcibly controls another, where scenes change, at extreme geometry, in growth and parameter systems, and where AI logic modes contradict.
how_to_apply: Estimate the test matrix early so you know where to prioritize. Put the first and heaviest passes on grabs, throws and restraints, especially on a target mid special move; on scene-changing supers (restrain, release, nothing leaks between scenes); on extreme and V-shaped terrain; and on every parameter, growth or unlock system. List the conditions each AI behavior mode responds to and test cases where two modes disagree. Let machines help: run CPU-versus-CPU battles overnight, and near the end pass save data between regions for worldwide testing.
anti_pattern: Brute-forcing combinations with no prioritization; holding the game to a completely bug-free standard.
example: Smash Ultimate's hot spots: grabbing a fighter mid special move, Final Smashes with scene changes, Stage Builder V-shaped terrain, Spirits (136). Overnight CPU battles and Japan, North America and Europe passing save data (208).
review_question: Which interactions in this build let one system seize control of another, and have they been tested first?
keywords: QA test planning combinatorial explosion test matrix edge cases risk-based testing automated testing bots soak test state conflicts

principle: Run bugs through tickets with repro steps, severity and the right owner
why: Having programmers playtest wastes their time, so projects use dedicated bug testers. Bugs found on the wrong version are not helpful and can cause problems. A ticket makes responsibility obvious and makes it less likely anything is overlooked. Programmers are not always the right fixers: artists fix character problems and animators fix animations. Visualizing tasks is vital.
how_to_apply: Require everyone to test on the latest daily build. Have testers work from design documents and checklists in subteams by game area. File a ticket only once the bug can be reproduced. A manager assigns a class (S for hangs or possible save corruption, A for progression blockers, lower classes sometimes waived on purpose) and routes it to the discipline that owns it. After a fix the tester confirms it in a variety of configurations, then marks it resolved rather than deleting it. Cross-reference or merge related tickets and rebalance overloaded people. Track all other work as tickets with one owner, a status and a deadline too.
anti_pattern: Reports from outdated builds; tickets with no repro steps; deleting closed tickets; tasks that live only in conversation.
example: Smash's bug-testing process (208); one character split into spec, model and rig, animation, programming, VFX, SFX and balancing tickets (94); bug reports with reproduction steps routed by one person (50).
review_question: Is every known bug a ticket with repro steps, a severity class, an owner and a verified fix?
keywords: bug tracking tickets severity triage bug reports reproduction steps QA workflow daily build issue tracker class S class A blocker crash save corruption

principle: Regression-test every fix, and keep late fixes narrow
why: Fixing one bug can introduce others, which is sometimes called enbugging, so even an urgent fix cannot ship right away; every fix means redoing plenty of other checks. Changing core systems late forces wide re-testing.
how_to_apply: Pair each fix with a regression pass over related systems before releasing a patch, and verify it in several configurations. For late or post-launch problems, prefer contained changes, such as lowering specific encounters or adding an easier option, over rewriting core AI or global difficulty code.
anti_pattern: Rushing a hotfix out without re-checking; touching core systems in a late patch when a narrow change would do.
example: Smash Ultimate's too-hard launch CPUs were addressed by lowering Challenger fight difficulty and adding Very Easy to World of Light, instead of changing core CPU functions (141).
review_question: What else could this fix break, and has that been re-checked?
keywords: regression testing hotfix patch enbugging fix verification contained fix late changes risk

principle: Ship as if no patch will come; treat updates as a bonus
why: Modern games are too complex to be perfect at release, every fix restarts testing so developers barely get to play the finished game, and the market is the best bug tester: a one-in-a-thousand bug will show up in a player's video. But no patch matters once players have given up. A completely bug-free standard belongs to banks and airports and would make releasing games practically impossible.
how_to_apply: Set release quality as though no update will ever ship. Lock content early enough to spend time on near-final builds. After launch, fix crashing and fatal bugs as a must, and weigh balance and quality-of-life updates as optional work against freeing the director and key staff for the next game. Watch player videos and reports as your biggest test pass. Budget the schedule for updates and DLC, which stretch it.
anti_pattern: Shipping rough on the assumption that patches will fix it; treating post-launch updates as free.
example: Smash for 3DS/Wii U released in fall to winter 2014 but development only wrapped in spring 2016 because of updates and DLC (135). The one-in-a-thousand bug that gets uploaded after launch (231).
review_question: If no patch ever shipped, would this build be acceptable to players on day one?
keywords: launch quality patches updates post-launch support day one patch content lock triage DLC schedule

principle: Fix the code before you tune the numbers
why: Even with correct parameters, mistakes in the code mean almost no amount of adjustment gives the result you want, which wastes the tuner's time. Even correct frame counts can be broken by code or data errors, and a trained sense of timing is how you notice.
how_to_apply: When tuning stops responding the way you expect, stop adjusting and have strong programmers hunt the underlying bugs. Play each move against its spec; when it feels off, inspect the code and data before touching the numbers.
anti_pattern: Tuning parameters on top of buggy code.
example: In Melee's final stretch, Satoru Iwata worked directly with the programmers to find code problems; without him Sakurai doubts it would have released before the end of 2001 (259).
review_question: When a parameter change does not produce the expected result, does anyone check the code before changing it again?
keywords: debugging tuning parameters code bugs balancing verification spec vs implementation frame data mismatch

principle: Name files so they sort sensibly and read at a glance
why: With a category-first scheme, anyone can read a name and know the move, and everything stays neat when sorted. Direction-first names or words for strength would make a huge mess when sorted. Names that are too short are easy to type but hard to understand. Romanized Japanese makes things harder for people who do not speak it: it is not just you who needs to understand your game.
how_to_apply: Define the scheme at project start: broad category first, then modifiers, then numbers for strength or sequence. Sort a folder by name and check related files group in a sensible order; if not, reorder the name parts. Use English when other or overseas teams may join. Test names on someone new to the project. Use one ID scheme across folders, files and tracking spreadsheets.
anti_pattern: Modifiers before the category; words for strength; cryptic abbreviations; romanized native-language names on international projects.
example: Smash labels: Attack11 to Attack13 for jab steps, Attack4 for smash, AttackS4 for side smash, AttackAirF for forward aerial, SpecialHi for up special, with N, Hi, S and Lw for directions (22). Sakurai's channel used category letter plus episode code for folders, files and the schedule (261).
review_question: Sorted alphabetically, do this folder's files group and order the way the team thinks about them?
keywords: file naming conventions asset naming labels sorting folders organization internal names English international teams

principle: Keep every file on a server with locking, merging and history
why: A large game is split into tens of thousands to millions of files with possibly hundreds of people editing them. Locking stops two people editing one file, but keeping a huge file locked to one person is inefficient, conflicting uploads still happen, and reversion, where changes vanish and the file returns to its old state, happens often. In theory there should be no issues; in practice it is a constant source of headaches.
how_to_apply: Put every file under a management tool on a server. Lock a file to edit it, upload when done to unlock. For large files several people need at once, allow simultaneous edits, let the tool merge, and name someone to resolve leftover conflicts by hand. When work goes missing, check version history first, since the tool backs up every edit.
anti_pattern: Passing copies around by hand; one person holding a huge file locked while others wait; assuming the tool makes lost work impossible.
example: General overview with no game-specific example (172).
review_question: If someone's change vanished today, could it be recovered from history, and who resolves merge conflicts?
keywords: version control source control file locking merge conflicts revert history backup asset management

principle: Treat a pre-release demo as a second build with its own QA
why: Demos are very effective at getting a game noticed, but if you are not careful one becomes almost another small game. People will find spoiler data left in a build, and removing data greatly raises the chance of breaking something. From the moment you decide on a demo you maintain two versions, and anything public needs nearly as much testing as the final game. A half-baked demo can get the game written off.
how_to_apply: Decide early and schedule the demo as its own deliverable with its own tuning, updates and near-full QA. Keep spoiler content in separable files so it can be stripped cleanly. Audit the demo build for leftovers, then retest thoroughly. Release a pre-launch demo only when it is balanced enough to represent the game; otherwise consider a post-launch demo and accept the smaller splash.
anti_pattern: Treating a demo as a quick slice; leaving spoiler data in it; releasing an unbalanced demo.
example: General advice; he contrasts pre-COVID expo demos with downloadable ones (122).
review_question: Could someone mining this demo's files find anything you have not announced?
keywords: demo build trial version spoilers datamining leaks separate build QA marketing demo

principle: Build CPU players from data and give them human reflexes
why: The computer has no eyes, so it must decide from data: the opponent's position and status, its own attack ranges, movement range and attack timing, and the opponent's attack data. CPUs that react faster than a human feel extremely unfair. Logic that switches mid-match can contradict itself, more often as criteria multiply. A CPU that perfect-shields every attack could be invincible, but that would not be fun.
how_to_apply: Convert each character's reach, attack timing and movement range into data the AI can query, and feed it the opponent's attack data, position and status. Add a reaction delay. Organize behavior into modes that switch with match state and test cases where two modes conflict. Tune high levels toward offense rather than waiting or perfect defense, and cap perfect blocks and dodges.
anti_pattern: Superhuman reaction speed; high-level CPUs that turtle; piling on behavior criteria without checking for contradictions.
example: Smash Ultimate's CPUs have a reflex delay, are briefly confused by reversed controls, and were tuned for offense over defense (221).
review_question: Can the CPU do anything a human physically could not, and where do its behavior modes disagree?
keywords: AI CPU opponents bots reaction time behavior modes decision data difficulty fairness fighting game AI

principle: Seed randomness with an unpredictable value
why: Computers can only do things in a predetermined way, so they cannot produce true randomness, and players can reset or repeat actions to always get the result they want.
how_to_apply: Factor the system's internal clock or another indefinite value into random number generation.
anti_pattern: Predictable random results that resetting can exploit.
example: General caution in his randomness episode (189).
review_question: Can a player reset or repeat an action to force a random outcome?
keywords: RNG random number generator seed manipulation reset abuse clock

principle: Match real-time online players within their local region
why: Smash needs fully synchronous communication, a major disadvantage compared with asynchronous games like Mario Kart, so lag makes it choppy unless players are close; higher input density makes online frame skips stand out. Matchmaking that is too narrow finds no one, while too broad gives lopsided matches.
how_to_apply: For synchronous games, matchmake within the local region, not just the country. Consider lowering input density where online play will lag. Tune matchmaking range against population, especially in low-population regions and hours.
anti_pattern: Country-wide or global matching for frame-tight synchronous play.
example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl's online play versus Mario Kart (108); Ultimate's matchmaking balance (170).
review_question: How far apart can two matched players be before the connection breaks the feel?
keywords: netcode online matchmaking latency region synchronous asynchronous lag online play

principle: Keep reference hardware, cables and displays organized and calibrated
why: Old games remain working tools for a developer, so they must be quick to reach. With many consoles connected, labels show what is plugged in where. Each monitor shows color slightly differently, which is fatal for art checks, and tinted office lighting skews art. Organizing is a pain, but it gets worse if you do not stay on top of it.
how_to_apply: Keep reference consoles connected through a selector, label every cable, adapter and selector input, give each console a switchable outlet and ventilation. Calibrate team monitors by eye against one shared reference screen and light review areas neutrally. Verify the display chain for lag before tests.
anti_pattern: Unlabeled tangles of cables; approving art on a monitor known to crush shadows.
example: Sakurai's custom six-door game cabinet with a selector and Tepra labels (216). A Mewtwo image losing its shadow on one monitor; an office lit yellow whose art came out bluish (184).
review_question: Can anyone on the team switch to any reference platform in minutes and trust the screen they are looking at?
keywords: dev environment reference library hardware setup cable labels monitor calibration test station organization
